summary: An informational discussion of the issues that arise for network-layer routing, especially unicast routing, when the Internet is run by many competing providers rather than a single backbone. It lays out the problems and considerations rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When many different companies each own a piece of the road, they must agree how cars travel between them. This memo talks about the problems of making those agreements work.

questions: how does routing work with multiple internet providers
what are the problems of multi-provider routing
why is renumbering needed with cidr
what are source and destination routing preferences
subtitle: An IAB discussion of what happens to Internet routing when many competing providers run the network.

tldr.problem: The Internet is no longer run by one backbone but by multiple Network Service Providers with different, sometimes conflicting goals and no central control, yet Internet-wide connectivity still needs cooperative routing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo does not define a protocol. It surveys issues: routing requirements, encapsulation, price structure, scalability, hierarchical routing and renumbering, and sharing routing information.
tldr.outcome: It ends with a list of further work, split into immediate, medium and long term, with renumbering and aggregation above the direct provider level as the most urgent.

today: RFC 1787 is an Informational memo offered by the IAB to stimulate discussion; the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol.

sections.title: Providers and Subscribers
sections.content:
Written by the author on behalf of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) to stimulate discussion, the memo starts from the network-layer service a provider offers: the set of destinations reachable through it. Because that value grows with the number of destinations, providers want to interconnect. A provider need not offer the same set to every subscriber.

Providers differ widely. Some serve one group, some accept anyone who pays, some restrict reselling, some are regulated and some are not, and their coverage ranges from a town to intercontinental. There is no centralized control, and providers often compete. Yet Internet-wide connectivity needs distributed routing across providers, so the providers' goals must be balanced against the public interest and subscribers' choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Many companies run different parts of the road and sometimes compete, but we all want to drive anywhere. They have to cooperate a little.

sections.title: Routing Requirements and Their Cost
sections.content:
Routing requirements fall into three categories: source preferences (the sender controls the path), destination preferences (the receiver controls the path to it) and constraints on transit traffic (a provider controls what crosses its routers and links). The degree of control can range from just having connectivity, to choosing immediate providers, to complete control over path selection.

The RFC argues about who pays. One organization should not be able to impose routing information overhead on others, and the cost of a requirement should not be borne by organizations that do not benefit. Organizations with simple needs should not carry the overhead of those with complex ones. The memo also notes that routing can be seen as a way for a provider to control who uses its services and for a subscriber to control the price it pays, and that a mechanism costing more than it saves is unlikely to survive in a competitive market.
sections.plainLanguage: Drivers, destinations and road owners all want a say in the route. Whoever wants special rules should pay for them, not everyone else.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Price Structure
sections.content:
Encapsulation creates a virtual IP overlay on top of existing infrastructure. With it a provider may no longer be able to limit transit traffic to certain sources or destinations, because the original addresses can be hidden inside another packet. Sources and destinations may also be unaware of the encapsulated part of a path, or have little control over it. The memo says further work is needed to understand these overlay effects.

Price structure also shapes routing: a provider can see routing as control over who uses its services, and a subscriber as control over the price it pays. The memo leaves the effect of different price structures as a long-term question.
sections.plainLanguage: If a package is wrapped inside another box, the road owners cannot see where it is really going, so their rules may not work.

sections.title: Scalability and Hierarchical Routing
sections.content:
Scalability is a key requirement, counted not just in memory, CPU and bandwidth but also in the human effort to operate the system. The need for CIDR already showed that routing which grows linearly with the number of networks or organizations is unacceptable, and it is unclear whether growth linear in the number of providers will be acceptable. The answer is powerful aggregation and abstraction, which minimizes inter-provider coordination but loses some routing information. That can hurt route optimality and even the ability to find an existing route. The memo suggests exploring on-demand acquisition of unaggregated information.

CIDR (RFC 1518 and RFC 1519) rests on hierarchical routing, which assumes addresses are "topologically significant" and, for most sites, provider-based. A subscriber that switches providers must change all of its addresses, a process called renumbering. DHCP helps but is not yet widely deployed, so more tools are needed, integrated with DNS. Hierarchical routing needs most, but not all, addresses to be topologically significant: a large organization could use a small number of provider-independent prefixes. Multi-homed subscribers, connected to more than one provider, are handled by CIDR in several ways that need more operational experience. Geography-based addresses are discussed as an alternative, but they require either topology that matches geography or non-topological addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses work like street addresses grouped by town, so mail sorters need few rules. If you move to another town, your address has to change too.

sections.title: Information Sharing and Further Work
sections.content:
As Internet-wide coordination gets harder, sharing information about routing requirements across organizational boundaries could improve stability and consistency, from troubleshooting to finding conflicting requirements. Because of the Internet's scale this information should be distributed, and the memo notes that work was underway to set up depositories called Routing Registries.

The summary lists what the IAB wants the community to look at. Immediate: technologies that make renumbering easier, and whether routing information aggregation above the direct provider level is feasible. Medium term: the relative importance of routing requirements, their impact on scalability, and alternatives to hierarchical routing. Long term: routing information sharing, overlays created by encapsulation, price structures, and balancing provider goals with the public interest. The conclusion adds that multicast routing, mobile hosts and large shared media such as ATM are not covered, and that the impact goes beyond routing into network management and troubleshooting.

The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road owners shared their rules with each other, fixing traffic jams would be easier. The memo ends with a to-do list, with the most urgent items first.

items.title: Source preferences
items.text: The originator of a packet controls the path to a destination.

items.title: Destination preferences
items.text: A destination controls the path from a source to it.

items.title: Transit constraints
items.text: A provider controls which traffic crosses its routers and links.
